abstract: Prolonged mechanical-induced stress (MIS) primes juvenile Arabidopsis plants for enhanced resistance against necrotrophic pathogens through the activation of jasmonate-mediated defense pathways. We hypothesised that MIS would weaken defense against hemibiotrophic pathogens that exploit jasmonate pathways to promote infection. We show that touch-acclimated wild-type plants were more susceptible to Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. conglutinans (Foc) infection than un-touched control plants. Jasmonic acid (JA) levels as well as JA defense-related gene expression were hyper-induced for up to 5 days post-inoculation in the MIS plants. In contrast, the MIS- and control- JA biosynthesis-deficient mutant jasmonate resistance 1 (jar1-11) was more resistant to Foc infection compared to the WT. The jar1-11 mutant showed significant attenuation in the induction of JA defense-responsive gene expression. In the absence of Foc infection, a single event of MIS similarly induced JA biosynthesis and stress-associated marker genes, but not JA signalling genes, in naive and touch-acclimated plant tissues. Touch-acclimated plants had higher basal levels of JA and JA defense-related genes expression, including PDF1.2, VSP1, and LOX1. Our findings highlight that prolonged MIS of Arabidopsis cross-primes JA-dependent susceptibility to a hemibiotrophic pathogen that can hijack the JA pathway to promote infection, revealing a potential trade-off when utilising MIS to promote immunity against necrotrophic pathogens or alter morphological traits for agronomical gains.
